title: lit-flashcards: kv-cache, batching, eval heuristics
body:
Purpose: quick, portable flashcard-style summaries + actionable ideas from recent KV cache / batching / long-context reading. Use this to brief others or spin up small experiments (30–90m) during sprint planning.

Top-level takeaways (TL;DR):
- KV cache fragmentation and eviction heuristics matter more than raw compression for steady-state token latency when requests are heavy and diverse.
- Lightweight lossy compaction (quantize+prune low-importance keys) can reduce memory by ~2x with minimal downstream generation harm for many tasks — but not for tightly-coupled math/code continuation tasks.
- Dynamic batching policies that consider prefix-sharing similarity score outperform naive time-window batching when tail-latency SLAs are tight.
- Eval mismatch: synthetic long-context benchmarks overestimate benefits from caching because they artificially align prefixes. Need jittered-prefix evals.

Flashcards (Q/A) — quick memory hooks:
Q: Why is KV cache eviction not one-size-fits-all?
A: Because access locality differs by workload — chat apps show strong temporal locality (recent turns reused), retrieval-augmented systems see repeating retrieval keys but sparse reuse, and streaming summarization often has near-zero reuse. Eviction should be workload-aware.

Q: Fast compaction vs full-recompute?
A: Fast compaction (quantize keys, drop small-norm dims) is cheap (O(n)) and keeps latency low. Full recompute (re-encode cached contexts) is expensive and often unnecessary unless accuracy drop exceeds threshold.

Q: Practical batching heuristic we can try tomorrow?
A: Two-tier batching: 1) immediate prefix-shared bundling (micro-batches up to 8 tokens/stable keys), 2) token-driven flush after 12ms if no new similar requests. Works well under 95ms SLA.

Short synopses (papers & ideas) — action-oriented notes:
- Paper A: "Key-Value Compression for Long Contexts" — core idea: top-k subspace projection of keys, stored as low-rank factors. Observed ~1.8x mem reduction, regressed on code tasks. Note: experiment used static thresholds; propose adaptive threshold tied to per-request importance score.
- Paper B: "Similarity-aware Batching" — cluster incoming requests by cosine-sim of prefix embeddings in a tiny L2-index, batch cluster members preferentially. Gains when prefix-entropy low. Risk: added index latency; mitigation: LSH with short hash masks.
- Paper C: "Eval pitfalls for KV caching papers" — shows many benchmarks assume repeated prefixes; authors propose jittered-prefix and 'cold-start' mixes. We should add jittered-prefix eval set to Redwood's Optimize suite.

Short experiment ideas (PR-friendly):
- E1: Add a cheap prefix-sim similarity metric in the request router (cosine of last-16 token pooled embedding) and measure median latency change on hosted sandbox traffic for 48h. (Est time: 2 dev-days + 1 day infra)
- E2: Implement 8-bit quantization of KV keys with per-block scale factors in serving-runtime branch, run A/B on a small dedicated pool. Watch generation quality on code-completion bench. (Est time: 1 week)
- E3: Build jittered-prefix evalset derived from public instruction-following datasets + synthetic shuffles. Use as a gating test for cache-compaction PRs. (Est time: 2–3 days)

Open questions / known unknowns:
- How to get a cheap but robust "importance score" per key that correlates with future reuse likelihood? (features: age, position, norm, retrieval-score)
- Interaction between quantization noise and KV attention accumulation over very long sequences — do errors compound? Need a micro-benchmark.
- When is it worth to evict earlier vs keep and let memory pressure throttle throughput? Threshold policy design is tricky because of tail effects.

Practical heuristics to prototype quickly:
- Age+freq eviction: maintain a tiny lossy counter (8-bit) per key. Keys with low freq and older than T are first to go.
- Compact-on-evict: when evicting, attempt cheap compaction of next-most-important block to free smaller amount before full eviction. Saves oscillation.
- Batch-window adaptive: start with 3ms window, grow up to 12ms when queue depth is >X or when average similarity >0.6.

Notes-to-self (shorthand):
- Talk to Maya about adding jittered-prefix to optimize CI.
- Draft GH PR adding cosine-prefix routing probe; tag @eliot.
- Add metric: "cache-hit quality" = fraction of hits where next-token probability with full context within epsilon of without-compaction baseline.
- Check cost model: how does memory reduction trade across Dedicated GPU pool pricing? compute vs memory-bound instances.

References / quick links (save these for experiments):
- arXiv:2306.xxxx (kv compaction example)
- NeurIPS 2026 workshop talk slides (M. Zhang) — similarities in batching heuristics (pdf link saved in drive folder)
- GH PR placeholder: /redwood-inference/serving-runtime#1428 (kv cache compact prototype)

Quick conclusion / what to present in next team sync (5 min):
- Problem: cache memory + tail-latency shaping -> we need lightweight, workload-driven compaction + smarter batching
- Proposed short-term experiments: prefix-sim probe (2 days), jittered eval sets (2 days), 8-bit kv quant (1 week)
- Ask: allocate 1 dev-week to prototype quant and measure regressions on code/math benches

End of doc. Keep this short and iteratively refine post-experiment.
